author: Adam Engel
title: Why Wyoming volleyball emphasized mental health in win over Air Force - NewsBreak
text:
By Adam Engel ,
5 hours ago
LARAMIE — Not even 72 hours passed since Lane Johnson stepped back.
Johnson — long considered one of the NFL’s most decorated right tackles — prioritized mental health when he retired Tuesday.
He stopped four weeks into his 14-season NFL career as a Philadelphia Eagle — one that included two Super Bowl wins and six Pro Bowl selections — citing the importance to “focus on my mental health ,” he wrote via Instagram.
Some, especially ESPN talking head Stephen A. Smith, ripped the decision.
So, when Johnson shut out football for good, it became the latest shift of high-profile athletes unashamed to admit their challenges. It also, coincidentally, aligned with student-athlete mental health week.
Some 1,700 miles west, the University of Wyoming volleyball team provided clear intention — mental health matters.
The Cowgirls stopped Air Force, 25-21, 22-25, 25-23, 25-23 during the Student-Athlete Mental Health match Thursday night at the UniWyo Sports Complex.
The team recognized student-athlete mental health week with pre-match shirts that read “Mental Health Matters” on the back and included a green No. 3 ribbon from the Hilinski’s Hope Foundation.
Green represents mental health awareness, while the No. 3 honors Washington State quarterback Tyler Hilinski, who died by suicide in 2018.
“(Mental health awareness) is huge, and it has made an improvement in all of athletics that people are talking about it,” Cowgirls coach Kaylee Prigge said.
Freshman middle blocker Rylee Heinz paced the Cowgirls (9-7 overall, 2-3 Mountain West) with 13 kills, while Emma Winter and Paige Lauterwasser joined with 11 and 10 kills, respectively.
The Cowgirls hit .228 and outkilled the Falcons, 62-51. It marked UW’s second consecutive win after it started conference play 0-3.
“Wins always feel good,” Prigge said. “Air Force is a really worthy opponent. I just don’t think they go away. There is a reason they are climbing back in every single set.”
Prigge played for NCAA Division II Tampa from 2010-12 — a time when mental health “was not something that was talked about really at all,” she said.
She joked that at DII, teammates’ mothers made sandwiches — a far cry from the catered meals the Cowgirls devour.
“We did not have the resources that we have here,” Prigge said. “It is also a product of the time … We definitely did not have any (mental health) resources when I played, and to now see where we are at (is special).”
UW director of student-athlete well-being Tedder Easton and assistant director of student-athlete well-being Chrislyn Cool are viewed as a huge part of the program, Prigge said.
A serious shift in the way athletes and coaches view mental health — in Prigge’s perspective — occurred in 2018 when five-time NBA all-star Kevin Love penned a Players’ Tribune article disclosing his experience with panic attacks.
“Mental health isn’t just an athlete thing,” Love wrote. “What you do for a living doesn’t have to define who you are. This is an everyone thing.”
Prigge, though, didn’t experience an approach to mental health that impacted her until she arrived in Laramie and noticed UW’s office of student-athlete well-being.
The Cowgirls also work with Max Out Mindset — a company that provides weekly mindset training to the team.
“(Mental health awareness) is so important,” Lauterwasser said. “As athletes, we put so much pressure on ourselves. We have to understand that we are parts of teams for a reason — to have them to lean on. Not just our teammates, but our coaches and our trainers.
“It is important that we know that we have those people to reach out to and those resources that are for us. It is great that people are paying more attention to that.”
Air Force’s (6-10, 2-3) Alysa Walker generated a match-high 21 kills — 11 more than teammate Annamaria Ramos.
UW, once it secured a 7-6 first-set lead, never relinquished it, thanks in part to a .231 hitting clip in the first frame.
The Cowgirls got within 22-21 in the second set, but couldn’t recover from a 15-11 deficit in that frame.
“We kind of relaxed in the second set,” Prigge said. “We are still learning that lesson. We cannot afford to do that. We have got to be on our jobs every single point.”
A kill from Winter clinched the third set, which capitalized a 14-9 UW run.
“Emma Winter started not really herself,” Prigge said. “I am really proud of the way she dug herself out of it and ended really strong.”
Abi Milby’s kill ended the match.
Redshirt junior middle blocker Evelyn Udezue participated in warmups for the first time since tearing her left anterior cruciate ligament on Sept. 25, 2025.
The Cowgirls visit Air Force at 2 p.m. Saturday.

A serious shift in the way athletes and coaches view mental health — in Prigge’s perspective — occurred in 2018 when five-time NBA all-star Kevin Love penned a Players’ Tribune article disclosing his experience with panic attacks.
